title: Where Did Human Equality Come From?

keyTerms.d: The conviction — held almost without having to be told — that every human being is of equal worth: the newborn and the dying, the genius and the person with a profound disability, the celebrated and the destitute. Strip away rank, usefulness, intelligence and strength, and a bare human worth remains, the same in each, outranking everything else about them. We treat its denial not as a mistake of fact but as a kind of blasphemy — “dehumanising.” It is a value, not a measurement.

The decisive distinction. As a measurement equal worth is plainly false: human beings are radically unequal in every capacity you can name — strength, health, intellect, beauty, longevity, usefulness to others — and nothing you can weigh, count or test comes out equal. “Equal worth” is a claim about what a person is, laid over a mass of evidence that they are not equal in what they can do. That it feels self-evident is itself the thing to explain, not evidence that it is natural.

The claim that God made humanity — not the king, not the free man, not the Greek, but humanity, male and female alike — in his own image, so that worth is not earned or measured but conferred, bestowed on every human being by the Maker, and therefore identical in each regardless of capacity or rank. Its root is not first of all Christian but Jewish: the doctrine developed in Jewish scripture and Jewish interpretation and stands on its own feet. The church did not invent it; what it did was carry it into the Gentile world at scale.

The core of ancient thinking (Larry Siedentop): the assumption that some human beings are higher and others lower not by accident of circumstance but by nature, from birth, in their very constitution. Aristotle states it as plain description — “from the hour of their birth, some are marked out for subjection, others for rule.” Ancient justice ranked persons, keeping each in the tier nature assigned; modern justice equalises. They are nearly opposite ideas wearing the same word.

Crucifixion was Rome’s instrument for erasing a human being’s standing — the death reserved for slaves and rebels, engineered to strip its victim of dignity in public. And Christians said that God the Son, in his true human nature, had been executed by that very method (said of the one divine person without implying that the divine nature suffered or that the Father was crucified). The empire’s supreme act of contempt became the object of worship — the Alexamenos graffito jeers at exactly this — and a civilisation that came to adore as God a man put to a slave’s death could no longer coherently hold the humiliated contemptible.

The bounded shape of the whole claim. Tracing where a value came from tells you its history and its cost; it never by itself tells you the creed it grew from is true. A belief can have a noble pedigree and still be false, and the case for the faith’s truth rests above all on the resurrection and the historical and philosophical arguments made throughout the Library, not on its social fruit. But “not a proof” is not “not evidence.”

The atheist historian Yuval Noah Harari grants the premise from the far side of the aisle: “there are no such things as rights in biology,” and “Homo sapiens has no natural rights, just as spiders, hyenas and chimpanzees have no natural rights.” Equality, in his account, is a conviction inherited from a Christian framework, not a fact you can find in the world. He is quoted only for the premise he shares — that equal worth is not written into nature — not for his own conclusion, that equality and rights are useful fictions, which this argument rejects.

The precise scope of the historical claim. The conviction did not travel a straight or purely churchly road: much of its modern legal and political articulation came through the Enlightenment, sometimes phrased against the church and in a deliberately secular idiom of natural rights. The claim here is narrower, and about origins rather than custody — that the load-bearing premise those later thinkers inherited and secularised, that every person carries an equal and unearned worth, entered the Western imagination through the image of God and had no other stable home in the ancient world.

derive.q: Equal worth feels self-evident. But tested as a measurement — strength, health, intellect, usefulness — is it actually true?
derive.ans: no — humans are radically unequal in every capacity you can weigh or test
derive.why: It is a value, not a measurement — because as a measurement it is plainly false. Human beings are radically unequal in every capacity you can name: in strength, health, intellect, beauty, longevity, usefulness to others. Nothing you can weigh, count or test comes out equal. “Equal worth” is a claim about what a person is, laid over a mass of evidence that they are not equal in what they can do.

derive.q: So equal worth cannot be read off nature — it is a value that had to come from somewhere. Did the ancient world that gave the West its philosophy already hold it?
derive.ans: no — it assumed natural inequality, something close to the opposite
derive.why: For most of recorded history almost no one believed it, and the civilisations that gave the West its philosophy believed something close to its opposite. The intellectual historian Larry Siedentop puts the point flatly: “the core of ancient thinking” was “the assumption of natural inequality.” Aristotle states it without embarrassment, as the furniture of the universe: some are marked out from birth for rule, others for subjection.

derive.q: The conviction entered the West through the claim that every human bears the image of God. Is that a Christian invention?
derive.ans: no — its root is Jewish; the church carried it, it did not invent it
derive.why: Its root is not first of all Christian but Jewish: the opening page of Genesis says God made humanity, male and female alike, in his own image, so worth is conferred, not earned, and identical in each regardless of capacity or rank. That doctrine developed in Jewish scripture and Jewish interpretation, and it stands on its own feet; the church did not invent it. What the church did was carry it into the Gentile world at scale.

derive.q: Grant the whole genealogy — equal worth entered the West through the image of God. Does that prove Christianity is true?
derive.ans: no — a genealogy of a value is not a proof of a creed
derive.why: On its own this is no proof of the creed: a belief can have a noble pedigree and still be false, and the case for the faith’s truth rests above all on the resurrection and the historical and philosophical arguments made throughout the Library, not on its social fruit. But “not a proof” is not “not evidence.”

derive.q: Then what does this line of evidence reach, taken entirely by itself?
derive.ans: a moral source above nature, shared with Judaism — pointing toward, not proving, the God the resurrection reveals
derive.why: The load-bearing premise — that every person carries an equal, unearned worth — is one no one can read off biology and is hard to ground in a universe with no God behind it. That step is contested, and worth granting honestly: some philosophers hold such worth simply obtains with no God, and the Christian’s claim is the modest one, that a Maker who confers it explains the conviction better than leaving it a brute fact. Taken by itself this line of evidence reaches a moral source above nature — a step toward God, shared with Judaism, not yet the resurrection, but pointing toward the same God the resurrection reveals.

honestState.p1: It is worth being exact about the size of the claim in both directions, because the temptation is to make it do either too much or too little. On its own this is no proof of the creed: a belief can have a noble pedigree and still be false, and the case for the faith’s truth rests above all on the resurrection and the historical and philosophical arguments made throughout the Library, not on its social fruit. But “not a proof” is not “not evidence”: the load-bearing premise — that every person carries an equal, unearned worth — is one no one can read off biology and is hard to ground in a universe with no God behind it. That step is contested, and worth granting honestly: some philosophers hold such worth simply obtains with no God, as a brute fact, and the Christian’s claim is the modest one, that a Maker who confers it explains the conviction better than leaving it a brute fact.
honestState.fairness: The premise is conceded from the far side of the aisle by the atheist historian Yuval Noah Harari (“there are no such things as rights in biology”), who nonetheless draws a conclusion Christians reject — that equality is a useful fiction with no ground in reality. Larry Siedentop’s larger thesis, that Christianity is where the equal individual was first thought, is itself debated among historians of political thought; the narrower point drawn on here, that the dominant strand of ancient thought assumed natural inequality, is widely accepted. Nicholas Wolterstorff’s grounding of inherent rights in a worth bestowed by God, and Brian Tierney’s canon-law genealogy of natural rights, are contested theses within the philosophy and history of rights, cited as the most developed scholarly statements of the case, not as settled results. Some philosophers hold equal worth simply obtains with no God. And the church has been a repeated traitor to its own doctrine — it blessed slaveholding, tolerated caste, and turned on the Jewish people from whom it had received the teaching of the image of God; Mark Noll documents the American slavery debate as a genuine crisis of biblical interpretation.
honestState.verdict: So when you find yourself certain — as you should be — that a trafficked child and a titan of industry are of exactly equal worth, that the strong owe something to the weak simply because they are human, you are not stating a fact of biology or a deliverance of pure reason. You are standing at the end of a long and improbable history, most of which ran the other way. The conviction of equal, unearned worth entered the Western imagination through the image of God — Jewish in root, carried by the church — and had no other stable home in the ancient world. That is a genealogy of a value, not a proof of a creed: on its own it is no proof of the faith, which rests above all on the resurrection. But it is not nothing — equal worth is hard to ground in a universe with no God behind it, so taken by itself this line of evidence reaches a moral source above nature, shared with Judaism, pointing toward the same God the resurrection reveals.

order: Human equality — that every person has an equal, unearned worth — is a value, not a biological fact: human beings are radically unequal in every measurable capacity, so equal worth cannot be read off from nature (as even the atheist Harari concedes).

This conviction was not the default of the ancient world, which assumed natural inequality; it entered the Western imagination through the Jewish, then Christian, claim that every human bears the image of God, and had no other stable home in antiquity.

Therefore the conviction of equal worth has deep Jewish and Christian roots — a genealogy of the value, not a proof of the creed: a belief can have a noble pedigree and still be false, and the case for the faith’s truth rests above all on the resurrection; but it is not nothing — equal, unearned worth is hard to ground in a universe with no God behind it (some hold it needs none, as a brute fact; the Christian answers that a moral source explains it better), a step toward a moral source above nature (shared with Judaism), pointing toward the same God the resurrection reveals.

cards.q: State Premise 1 — and its precision check.
cards.a: Equal worth is a value, not a biological fact. Precision: human beings are radically unequal in every measurable capacity — strength, health, intellect, longevity, usefulness — so “equal worth” is a claim about what a person is, laid over the evidence that they are not equal in what they can do. It cannot be read off nature; even the atheist Harari grants there are no such things as rights in biology.

cards.q: State Premise 2 — and its precision check.
cards.a: The conviction was not the ancient world’s default — that world assumed natural inequality. Equal worth entered the West through the Jewish, then Christian, claim that every human bears the image of God, and had no other stable home in antiquity. Precision: a claim about origins, not custody — much of the modern articulation came through the Enlightenment, but the load-bearing premise entered through the image of God. The root is Jewish; the church did not invent it.

cards.q: What does the conclusion reach — and what does it NOT reach?
cards.a: It reaches that the conviction of equal worth has deep Jewish and Christian roots — a genealogy of the value. It does NOT reach that Christianity is true: a belief can have a noble pedigree and still be false, and the case for the faith rests above all on the resurrection, not its social fruit. But “not a proof” is not “not evidence.”

cards.q: Why is equal worth a value and not a measurement?
cards.a: Because as a measurement it is plainly false: people differ in every capacity you can weigh, count or test — nothing comes out equal. “Equal worth” is a claim about what a person is, laid over a mass of evidence that they are not equal in what they can do. Its feeling of obviousness is itself the thing to explain.

cards.q: Why is the image of God credited to Judaism, not treated as a Christian invention?
cards.a: Because the doctrine that every human bears God’s image developed in Jewish scripture and Jewish interpretation and stands on its own feet: Genesis says God made humanity, male and female alike, in his own image, so worth is conferred, not earned, and identical in each. The church did not invent it — what it did was carry it into the Gentile world at scale.

cards.q: What did the cross do to the ancient logic of contempt?
cards.a: Crucifixion was Rome’s instrument for erasing a human being’s standing — the death reserved for slaves and rebels, engineered to strip dignity in public. Christians said God the Son, in his true human nature, had been executed by that method, so the empire’s supreme act of contempt became the object of worship. A civilisation that came to adore a crucified man as God could no longer coherently hold the humiliated contemptible — whatever it went on doing in practice.

cards.q: What does “a genealogy, not a proof” rule IN — and rule OUT?
cards.a: It rules IN that equal worth is not simply obvious or natural but was won, against the grain of the world, through the image of God — a real line of evidence. It rules OUT the claim that this history proves Christianity true: a belief can have honourable roots and still be false, and the case for the faith rests above all on the resurrection.

cards.q: Harari is an atheist. Why quote him, and for what exactly?
cards.a: For the premise, not the conclusion. He grants, from the far side of the aisle, that “there are no such things as rights in biology” — equal worth is not a fact of nature. He is NOT quoted for his own conclusion, that equality and rights are useful fictions with no ground in reality, which this argument rejects.

cards.q: The sceptic says equality is “just obvious.” What is wrong with that move?
cards.a: The feeling of obviousness is itself the thing to explain. As a measurement equal worth is false, and for most of history most societies believed the reverse — some are marked out from birth for rule, others for subjection. A conviction won against the grain of the world is not the mind’s default; its obviousness shows how completely one particular inheritance has soaked into the air we breathe.

cards.q: Some ancient voices reached toward a common humanity. Why doesn’t that sink Premise 2?
cards.a: Because two things are true of them: they grounded common humanity in a shared nature rather than in a worth bestowed on each, and — decisively — none became a movement, a law, or a settled conviction. Seneca kept his slaves; Ulpian’s maxim sat inside a code that enforced slavery. The dissent lived as an idea and never became anything more.

cards.q: The church enslaved people. How can it claim credit for equality?
cards.a: The failures are real, and no account of where the standard came from lessens them. But we can call the betrayals betrayals only because there was a standard to betray — and it was, in no small part, the church’s own standard that reformers turned back against it: abolitionists indicted Christian slaveholders from Genesis and the image of God, even as others marshalled Scripture to defend slavery, in a genuine crisis of biblical interpretation. The ideal judged its own failures and armed its own critics.

cards.q: What does this line of evidence reach, taken entirely by itself?
cards.a: A moral source above nature — a step toward God, shared with Judaism, not yet the resurrection but pointing toward the same God the resurrection reveals. It does NOT by itself reach the Triune God or prove the creed. The step is contested: some hold equal worth simply obtains with no God, and the Christian’s claim is the modest one — that a Maker who confers it explains the conviction better than leaving it a brute fact.

obj.q: Human equality is just obvious — any decent person recoils at treating people as unequal and calls it “dehumanising.” You don’t need a religion or a history lesson to see that everyone is of equal worth.
obj.model: The feeling of obviousness is itself the thing to explain. As a measurement equal worth is false — humans differ in every testable way. For most of history most societies did not believe it, and the ancient world often believed the reverse: Aristotle held some are marked out from birth for rule, others for subjection. A conviction that had to be won against the grain of the world is not the default setting of the human mind. Its obviousness to a modern Westerner is not evidence that it is natural — it is evidence of how completely one particular inheritance has soaked into the air we breathe.

obj.q: If the best thing in the modern moral world came from the faith, doesn’t that show the faith is true? A tree is known by its fruit.
obj.model: No — and this track does not claim it does. This is a genealogy of a conviction, not a demonstration of a creed. A belief can have deep and honourable roots and still be false; that equal human worth has Christian and Jewish origins tells you where the standard came from. On its own it is no proof — but it is not nothing: equal, unearned worth is hard to ground in a universe with no God behind it. The case for the faith’s truth rests on other grounds — the resurrection and the arguments made elsewhere in the Library — not on its social fruit.

obj.q: Some Stoics and jurists reached toward it: Seneca could call a slave a fellow human being, and the jurist Ulpian recorded that by natural law all human beings are equal. The idea was already there.
obj.model: Those voices were real, and honesty names them. But two things are true of them: they grounded common humanity in a shared nature (for the Stoics, a shared capacity, reason) rather than in a worth bestowed on each, and — decisively — none became a movement, a law, or a settled conviction. Seneca kept his slaves; Ulpian’s maxim sat inside a code that enforced slavery. The dissent lived as an idea and never became anything more. The idea that every human being has an equal, inviolable worth simply by being human entered Western law and sentiment largely through a different route.

obj.q: A conviction can have Christian roots and still be a human invention that outgrew them; and the church blessed slaveholding, tolerated caste, turned on the Jewish people from whom it had received the teaching of the image of God, and looked away from cruelties its own scriptures condemned.
obj.model: The pedigree point is correct, and this track concedes it in our own voice: on its own this is no proof of the creed — a belief can have a noble pedigree and still be false, and the case for the faith’s truth rests above all on the resurrection. But “not a proof” is not “not evidence.” The church’s failures are real, and no account of where the standard came from lessens them. Yet we can call the church’s betrayals betrayals only because there was a standard to betray — and it was, in no small part, the church’s own standard that the reformers turned back against it. Many abolitionists indicted Christian slaveholders from Genesis and the image of God, even as other Christians marshalled Scripture to defend slavery, in what became a genuine crisis of biblical interpretation. The ideal judged its own failures and armed its own critics. Taken by itself this line of evidence reaches a moral source above nature — a step toward God, shared with Judaism, not yet the resurrection, but pointing toward the same God the resurrection reveals.

unseen.q: Even in Aristotle’s own day, Greeks argued that slavery was a mere human convention, contrary to nature — the very position he wrote his defence of natural slavery against. So an equal-nature intuition was already present in antiquity; it is not a uniquely Jewish or Christian inheritance at all.
unseen.model: Honesty requires naming the dissent, and the essay does: Aristotle argues for natural slavery precisely because others in his own day were calling slavery a mere human convention, contrary to nature. But that cuts the other way — that Aristotle had to argue for natural inequality shows it was the dominant assumption he was defending. And here is the decisive fact: none of that dissent became a movement, a law, or a settled conviction that the weak have a claim on the strong simply by being human. Seneca kept his slaves; the jurist Ulpian’s maxim that by natural law all human beings are equal sat inside a legal code that enforced slavery. The dissent lived as an idea and never became anything more. The conviction that every person carries an equal, unearned worth — conferred rather than earned, and identical in each — entered Western law and sentiment largely through a different route: the image of God, Jewish in root and carried by the church into the Gentile world.
